## Introduction

In this lab, I will apply count regression to investigate the factors associated with how often older adults visit a physician's office. Rather than fitting a single model, I will build up a Poisson model, check it with simulation-based residuals, move to a negative binomial (NB) model if the data call for it, decide whether the zeros need their own model, and then test and probe an interaction.

```{r}
#Set-up
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

# Data loading
data(NMES1988)

# Assign reference groups of average (health), male (gender), and no (insurance)
data <- NMES1988 |>
  select(visits, chronic, health, gender, school, insurance) |> 
  mutate(health = fct_relevel(factor(health), "average"),
         gender = fct_relevel(factor(gender), "male"),
         insurance = fct_relevel(factor(insurance), "no"))
```

The `NMES1988` data follows 4406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. The variables of interest are described below:

| Variable    | Description                                              |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `visits`    | **Outcome:** Number of physician office visits           |
| `chronic`   | Number of chronic conditions                             |
| `health`    | Self-perceived health: `poor`, `average`, or `excellent` |
| `gender`    | `male` or `female`                                       |
| `school`    | Years of education                                       |
| `insurance` | Covered by private insurance: `no` or `yes`              |

The reference groups are **Average Health**, **Male**, and **No Insurance**.

## Exploring the Data

```{r}
# Exploring the data
visits_summary <- data |> # Exploring descriptive stats for outcome
  summarise(n = n(),
    mean = mean(visits),
    var = var(visits),
    p_zero = mean(visits == 0), # Proportion of zero values
    max = max(visits))

gt(visits_summary) |> 
  cols_label(p_zero = "% 0s") |> 
   fmt_number(columns = c(mean, var, p_zero),
              decimals = 2)
```

As shown above, the outcome is a count (i.e., whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed), describing the number of physician's office visits for each person (mean = `r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`). Notably, the variance is `r round(visits_summary$var / visits_summary$mean, 2)` times the mean, suggesting overdispersion. Additionally, `r round(100 * visits_summary$p_zero)`% of the sample reported no visits, and `r sum(data$visits > 25)` individuals visited a physician more than 25 times in 1987-1988. See the plot below for the distribution of responses for this outcome.

```{r}
# Creating a plot of the overall distribution of the outcome variable (number of visits)
descriptive_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Physician's Office Visits", y = "Number of People")

descriptive_plot
```

The DHARMa plots, below, depict substantial violations of Gaussian assumptions, suggesting that a linear model would be a poor fit for the data. The QQ plot shows a significant deviation from the expected residual distribution (KS test *p* \< .001) and the residuals-versus-predicted plot reveals significant quantile deviations. Notably, if a linear model was used, it could predict negative article counts. Additionally, a Gaussian model assumes constant variance (i.e., puts mass on negative counts and too little mass at zeros) and treats effects as additive. On the other hand, count variance grows with the mean and it is more natural for a predictor to multiply the expected count.

```{r}
  # Fitting a Gaussian model to see why a linear model doesn't work for counts

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

#simulation 
set.seed(9041)
res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(m_gauss, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_gauss)
```

## Specifying Competing Count Models

I will fit an intercept-only model and two increasingly complex substantive models.

| Model | Formula | Research rationale |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| null: Null | `visits ~ 1` | Baseline model |
| one_pred: Chronic | `visits ~ chronic` | Number of visits varies with number of chronic conditions |
| full poisson: Full | `visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance` | Other predictors explain additional variation |

The models are **nested**: Each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one or more additional predictors.

```{r}
### Specifying competing count models
# Null (intercept-only) Poisson model: no predictors, just the overall average.
null <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# One-predictor Poisson model: does the number of chronic conditions predict physician visits?
one_pred <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# Full Poisson model: all five predictors at once.
poisson <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

tests <- anova(null, one_pred, poisson) # Comparing models

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |> # Selecting relevant stats from model comparison
  rename(Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(null) # More model-level statistics
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(one_pred)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(poisson)

mods <- c("M0: Null",
  "M1: Chronic",
  "M2: Full") # Naming models

glances <- rbind(glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2) # Combining individual glances into one object

comparison_table <- cbind(Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests) # Combining anova and glance results into one object

comparison_table |> #Formatting combined results into gt table
  select(Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat),
    decimals = 2) |>
  fmt(columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x)))}) |>
  sub_missing(columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—")
```

Based on the above model comparison statistics, the **Model 2** (i.e., the full model) seems to fit the data best. This is because the log-likelihood test for Model 2 is statistically significant, χ²(5) = 959.92, *p* \< .001, suggesting that it fits the data better than Model 1 (which also fits the data significantly better than the intercept-only model; χ²(1) = 2175.43, *p* \< .001). Additionally, Model 2 also has the lowest AIC and BIC values, indicating it has the best model fit, even when accounting for model complexity. As will be presented shortly, all of the predictors in Model 2 explain significant variability in the outcome, further highlighting its potential predictive value.

The degrees of freedom values reflect the difference in the number of parameters between a model and its precursor. The intercept-only model estimates the average number of physician's office visits without accounting for any predictors.

## Poisson Diagnostic Tests

```{r}
# Evaluating the Poisson Model
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

# Creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

# Case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(selected_name,
  "M0: Null" = null,
  "M1: Chronic" = one_pred,
  "M2: Full" = poisson)

# Setting a seed so the simulated residuals are reproducible
set.seed(9041)

# Simulating 500 new datasets from the fitted Poisson model.
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(poisson, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# Two diagnostic panels: QQ plot (points should follow the diagonal)
# and residuals vs. predicted values (should be flat)
plot(res_pois)
```
The diagnostic tests demonstrate, however, that a Poisson regression model does not adequately fit the data. The QQ plot below shows that the observed residuals differ significantly from the expected uniform distribution, depicting an S-shaped pattern instead of following the diagonal reference line. The dispersion test is also significant, flagging that the variance exceeds the mean and violating the Poisson assumption that the variance is equal to the mean. The outlier test is also significant, further indicating that another count model other than Poisson may better fit the data. The right-hand plot also indicates assumption violations, as the residuals are clearly not uniformly distributed across the range of predicted values, with a Levene's test flagging significant heterogeneity in the variability of residuals.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Formal dispersion test: is the observed variance bigger (or smaller) than the Poisson model expects?
# A significant p means the variance = mean assumption doesn't hold
disp_pois <- testDispersion(res_pois)
disp_pois

# Zero-inflation test: does the data have more zeros than the Poisson predicts?
zi_pois <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)
zi_pois
```

The dispersion ratio is `r round(disp_pois$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_pois$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_pois$p.value, 3)))`), and there are `r round(zi_pois$statistic, 2)` times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows. This matters because a Poisson's standard errors assume variance = mean. When the data are overdispersed, those SEs are too small, CIs are too narrow, and *p*-values are too optimistic.

Although it may be tempting to fit a zero-inflation model based on the significant zero-inflation test, this test can only tell us that there is an abundance of zeros, but not their cause or how to treat them. This is particularly important to note, as a zero-inflated model treats zeros as coming from two distinct sources (i.e., structural and sampling), based on theoretical and empirical justifications. As a next step, then, I will fit and evaluate a negative binomial model, which may be better positioned to handle greater variability and excess zeros.

## Fitting Negative Binomial Model

```{r}
# Negative binomial (NB2) model
neg_binom <- glmmTMB(visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"))

# LRT: does the NB fit better than the Poisson?
lrt_nb<-anova(poisson, neg_binom)
gt(lrt_nb)
```

The negative binomial model fits the data significantly better than the Poisson model, χ²(`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. As the key distinction between the two models is that the negative binomial introduces an additional parameter that allows the variance to exceed the mean, as denoted by the additional degree of freedom, this suggests that the overdispersion detected in the poisson diagnostic tests was a major issue. If I had continued with the poisson model, reports of statistical significance for individual predictors may have been overstated and the standard errors and confidence intervals may have been overly narrow, potentially leading to misinformed substantive conclusions. It's worth noting that the coefficient estimates would have remained relatively similar. That said, diagnostic tests should also be run for the negative binomial model to examine whether excess zeros, influential observations, and uniformity of residuals remain issues of concern. 

## Negative Binomial Diagnostic Tests
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Same seed as before so the residuals are reproducible and comparable to the Poisson check.
set.seed(9041)

# If the NB is adequate, these should now be uniform, unlike the Poisson's.
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(neg_binom, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# QQ plot: points should now sit close to the diagonal.
# Residuals vs. predicted: should be roughly flat.
plot(res_nb)

# Dispersion: the ratio should now be close to 1 and non-significant.
disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)

# Zero inflation: does the NB reproduce the observed number of zeros?
# A non-significant result means the NB's extra variance already accounts for the zeros, so there's no need for a zero-inflated or hurdle model.
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)
```
As shown above, the negative binomial model resolved the overdispersion issue: The dispersion ratio is now `r round(disp_nb$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_nb$p.value, 3)))`), close to 1 and non-significant. However, the zero-inflation test found that there are `r round(zi_nb$statistic, 2)` times as many zeros as the negative binomial model expects (`r ifelse(zi_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(zi_nb$p.value, 3)))`). This may reflect why the KS and outlier tests remained significant, even as the QQ plot shows that the observed residuals are uniformly distributed across the expected range of values. As a result, I will fit a zero-inflation negative binomial model and compare it with a hurdle NB model to see which fits the data best.

See below for a visualization of the predicted number of physician's office visits (based on the additive negative binomial model), as predicted by the number of patients' chronic conditions. The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors because of the log link: Each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, which multiplies the expected count, so the same one-chronic-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

```{r}
# Predicted mean physician's office visits from the additive NB, on the count scale.
# "chronic [0:25]" plots visits from 0 to 25
pred_nb <- predict_response(neg_binom, terms = "chronic [0:25]")

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Number of Physician's Office Visits by Number of Chronic Conditions",
    x     = "Number of Chronic Conditions", y = "Visits")
```

## Comparing Zero-Inflation and Hurdle Negative Binomial Models
```{r}
# Zero-inflated NB with a constant zero-inflation probability
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ 1,
  data = data, family = nbinom2())

# Zero-inflated NB with predictors in the zero part
m_zinb_full <- glmmTMB(visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = nbinom2())

# Hurdle NB
m_hurd <- glmmTMB(visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2())

# Compare models
lrt_nb_zi <- anova(neg_binom, m_zinb_full)

# The hurdle isn't nested in the NB, so compare with AIC/BIC (lower = better)
nb_AIC <- AIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
nb_BIC <- BIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
```
It was not surprising to find that a full zero-inflation NB fits the data better than the standard NB model χ²(`r abs(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Chi Df"])`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_nb_zi[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. When looking at the AIC and BIC values, however, it appears that the hurdle NB model fits the data even better Specifically, although the zero-inflation model has similarly low AIC (`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_AIC[3, "AIC"])`) and BIC (`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_BIC[3, "BIC"])`) values, the hurdle model's AIC (`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_AIC[4, "AIC"])`) and BIC (`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_BIC[4, "BIC"])`) values are even lower.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Then re-check the chosen model with DHARMa
set.seed(9041)
res_hurd_nb <- simulateResiduals(m_hurd, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

res_hurd_nb_test <- testZeroInflation(res_hurd_nb)
```
Furthermore, the diagnostic tests also suggest that the hurdle NB model fits the data well, as the non-significant zero-inflation test suggests that this model already accounts for the zeros (statistic = `r round(res_hurd_nb_test$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(res_hurd_nb_test$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(res_hurd_nb_test$p.value, 3)))`).

## Testing and Probing an Interaction
Now that I've chosen a model, I will examine whether the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differs for people based on whether or not they have health insurance. I expect that for individuals with fewer chronic conditions, those who having insurance will predict a greater number of physician's office visits. For those with a larger number of chronic conditions, I expect that the distinction between those with and without health insurance will narrow significantly, as individuals with many chronic conditions may have less opportunity or desire to avoid or decline medical care due to the increased negative impact of multiple chronic conditions on their health and well-being. 
```{r}
# Hurdle NB model results
hurdle_results <- summary(m_hurd)

# Giving conditional results their own data frame and adding 95% CIs
hurdle_cond_results <- as.data.frame(hurdle_results$coefficients$cond) |> 
  mutate(CI_low = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`,
    CI_high = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`)

# Giving zero-inflated results their own data frame and adding 95% CIs
hurdle_zi_results <- as.data.frame(hurdle_results$coefficients$zi) |>
  mutate(CI_low = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`,
    CI_high = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`)

# Hurdle NB model with a chronic condition x insurance interaction.
# The other predictors are controls.
interact <- glmmTMB(visits ~ health + gender + school + chronic * insurance,
                    ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
                    data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2())

interaction_results <- as.data.frame(summary(interact)$coefficients$cond)

# LRT: does adding the interaction improve fit over the additive NB?
lrt_int <- anova(m_hurd, interact)
gt(lrt_int)
```
The interaction was not significant here, χ²(`r abs(lrt_int[2, "Chi Df"])`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_int[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`, but I will probe it below anyway to better understand the patterns of results and different levels of both chronic condition and insurance status.

```{r}
# Predicted mean number of visits from the interaction model, on the count scale.
pred_int <- predict_response(interact, terms = c("chronic", "insurance"), type = "count")

ggplot(pred_int, aes(x = x, y = predicted,
                                        colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
              alpha = .2, color = NA) + # Setting ribbon opacity and removing ribbon border
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "coral", yes = "green4")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(no = "coral", yes = "green4")) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Physician's Office Visits by Chronic Conditions and Insurance",
    x = "Number of Chronic Conditions",
    y = "Predicted Physician's Office Visits",
    colour = "Insurance",
    fill = "Insurance") +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Simple slopes: the slope of chronic estimated separately for those with and without health insurance.
slopes <- emtrends(interact, 
  specs = ~ insurance, 
  var = "chronic")

pairs_slopes <- as.data.frame(pairs(slopes))

#test simple slopes against zero
slopes_sum <- summary(slopes, infer = TRUE)

slopes_sum
```
Whereas the simple slopes coefficients estimate the association between number of chronic conditions and physicians' office visits separately for those with and without health insurance, the statistics (estimate, SE, *p*) from `pairs()` tests whether the two slopes (i.e., associations) differ. With only two levels of the moderator, this contrast reproduces the interaction coefficient from `summary(interact)` but with the opposite sign; `pairs()` computes no − yes, whereas simple slopes computes yes − no.

`ggeffects` (Step 3) holds categorical predictors at their respective reference levels, while `emmeans` *averages over* their levels. The insurance *contrasts* are equivalent in this case because with no interaction involving the other categorical predictors (i.e., health, gender), its effect cancels out of the comparison.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Simple effects: flip the probing around and look at the insurance difference at specific values of chronic condition number, instead of the chronic slope within each insurance response type

# Pick the probing values: low (-1 SD), average (mean) and high (+1 SD) chronic condition number
chronic_mean <- mean(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_sd <- sd(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_values <- chronic_mean + c(-1, 0, 1) * chronic_sd

# Estimated marginal means (EMMs) for each insurance response type at each chronic condition number value.
insurance_emmeans <- emmeans(interact,
  specs = ~ insurance | chronic,
  at = list(chronic = chronic_values))

# Estimated mean visits in each insurance x chronic cell.
summary(insurance_emmeans, type = "response")

# Insurance differences at each chronic value, on the log scale.
pairs(insurance_emmeans)

# Building a data frame of the simple effects
contrast_df <- summary(pairs(insurance_emmeans)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(chronic = rep(chronic_values, each = 1),
         chronic_level = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")[match(round(chronic, 6), round(chronic_values, 6))]) |>
  select(chronic_level, contrast, estimate, SE, z.ratio, p.value)
```
```{r}
# Formatting the dataframe as a table
contrast_df |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(chronic_level = "Number of Chronic Conditions", contrast = "Contrast",
    estimate = "Log Contrast", SE = "SE", z.ratio = "z", p.value = "p") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, SE, z.ratio), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = \(x) scales::pvalue(x, accuracy = 0.001, add_p = FALSE)) |>
  tab_header(title = "Simple Effects of Insurance Across Number of Chronic Conditions",
    subtitle = "Hurdle Negative-Binomial Regression") |>
  tab_source_note("Log contrast = No − Yes; z-tests and p-values are computed on the log scale.")
```
There is little evidence that the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician’s office visits differs according to health insurance status. Although the number of chronic conditions was significantly and positively associated with visits among both uninsured (*b* = `r round(slopes_sum$chronic.trend[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"], 3)))`) and insured individuals (*b* = `r round(slopes_sum$chronic.trend[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"], 3)))`), the difference between these slopes was not statistically significant (*b* = `r round(pairs_slopes$estimate, 2)`, *p* = `r round(pairs_slopes$p.value, 3)`). Expectedly, the interaction term corroborated that health status does not affect the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician’s office visits (b = `r round(interaction_results["chronic:insuranceyes", "Estimate"], 2)`, SE = `r round(interaction_results["chronic:insuranceyes", "Std. Error"], 2)`, z = `r round(interaction_results["chronic:insuranceyes", "z value"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(interaction_results["chronic:insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(interaction_results["chronic:insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"], 3)))`). Adding the interaction to the hurdle negative binomial model did not significantly improve model fit, χ²(`r abs(lrt_int[2, "Chi Df"])`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_int[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. The simple effects analysis (above) demonstrated that individuals with health insurance visited physicians' significantly more frequently across the three levels of chronic health conditions. Although there was a very slight downward trend in the associations as the number of chronic conditions increased, these findings do not establish interaction effects. Thus, the omnibus interaction test and probing results provided little support for insurance status moderating the relationship between chronic conditions and physician visits, suggesting low confidence in the interaction effect.

## Results
The current analysis investigated whether a variety of factors influenced the frequency of physicians' office visits in the U.S. 

#### Model Selection

The counts for visits were overdispersed (*M* = `r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`, *s*² = `r round(visits_summary$var, 2)`; `r round(100 * visits_summary$p_zero)`% zeros). Simulation-based residual checks on a Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = `r round(disp_pois$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(disp_pois$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_pois$p.value, 3)))`) and excess zeros (observed/expected = `r round(zi_pois$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(zi_pois$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(zi_pois$p.value, 3)))`). A negative binomial model fit significantly better, χ²(`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`, and showed no remaining evidence of overdispersion (ratio = `r round(disp_nb$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(disp_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_nb$p.value, 3)))`), but the zero-inflation test suggested that a separate model for zeros was needed (ratio = `r round(zi_nb$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(zi_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(zi_nb$p.value, 3)))`). A subsequent hurdle zero-inflation NB model was fitted, which fit the data significantly better than the standard NB model, χ²(`r abs(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Chi Df"])`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_nb_zi[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb_zi[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. After reviewing the AICs and BICs of the competing models, it was decided that the hurdle NB fit the data even better (AIC = `r sprintf("%.2f", nb_AIC[4, "AIC"])`, BIC = `r sprintf("%.2f", nb_BIC[4, "BIC"])`). The non-significant zero-inflation test further suggested that this model adequately accounts for the zeros (statistic = `r round(res_hurd_nb_test$statistic, 2)`, `r ifelse(res_hurd_nb_test$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(res_hurd_nb_test$p.value, 3)))`). Thus, the hurdle NB model was selected as the appropriate model for this exercise.

#### Main Effects

Noting that all associations were adjusted for the other predictors in the model, the results of the **conditional** model (i.e., those who had 1+ visits) found that the number of chronic health conditions was significantly and positively associated with the expected number of physician’s office visits (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["chronic", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["chronic", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["chronic", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_cond_results["chronic", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["chronic", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). Individuals with more chronic conditions reported more physician's office visits, holding the other predictors constant. 

Poor health was significantly associated with a higher expected number of physician visits relative to average health (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthpoor", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthpoor", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthpoor", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_cond_results["healthpoor", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["healthpoor", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). Conversely, excellent health was significantly associated with a lower expected number of visits relative to average health (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthexcellent", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthexcellent", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["healthexcellent", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_cond_results["healthexcellent", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["healthexcellent", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). 

Education was significantly and positively associated with the expected number of visits (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["school", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["school", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["school", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_cond_results["school", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["school", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). 

Similarly, individuals with health insurance had a higher expected number of visits than those without insurance (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["insuranceyes", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["insuranceyes", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["insuranceyes", "CI_high"])`], *p* = `r ifelse(hurdle_cond_results["insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). 

Gender was not significantly associated with the expected number of visits. Although females had a slightly higher expected number of visits than males, this difference was not statistically significant (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["genderfemale", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["genderfemale", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_cond_results["genderfemale", "CI_high"])`], *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_cond_results["genderfemale", "Pr(>|z|)"])`).

In the **zero-inflation component**, which compared those with zero visits to all others, the number of chronic conditions was significantly and negatively associated with the likelihood of reporting zero physician visits (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["chronic", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["chronic", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["chronic", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_zi_results["chronic", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["chronic", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). In other words, individuals with fewer chronic conditions had higher odds of reporting zero visits.

Excellent health was significantly and positively associated with the likelihood of reporting zero visits relative to average health (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthexcellent", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthexcellent", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthexcellent", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["healthexcellent", "Pr(>|z|)"])`). However, poor health was not significantly associated with the likelihood of reporting zero visits (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthpoor", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthpoor", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["healthpoor", "CI_high"])`], *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["healthpoor", "Pr(>|z|)"])`).

Education was also significantly and negatively associated with the likelihood of reporting zero visits (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["school", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["school", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["school", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_zi_results["school", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["school", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). 

Similarly, individuals with health insurance had significantly lower odds of reporting zero visits than those without insurance (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["insuranceyes", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["insuranceyes", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["insuranceyes", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_zi_results["insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["insuranceyes", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`).

Females had significantly lower odds of reporting zero physician visits than males (*b* = `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["genderfemale", "Estimate"])`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["genderfemale", "CI_low"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", hurdle_zi_results["genderfemale", "CI_high"])`], *p* `r ifelse(hurdle_zi_results["genderfemale", "Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", hurdle_zi_results["genderfemale", "Pr(>|z|)"]))`). 
As with the conditional model, all associations in the zero-inflation component were adjusted for the other predictors in the model.

#### Interaction

Adding a Chronic Conditions × Insurance Status interaction did not significantly improve fit, χ²(`r abs(lrt_int[2, "Chi Df"])`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_int[2, "Chisq"])`, `r ifelse(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. Simple slopes showed that the number of chronic conditions was significantly associated with the number of physician's office visits both for those with health insurance (*b* = `r round(slopes_sum$chronic.trend[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"], 2)`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", slopes_sum$asymp.LCL[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", slopes_sum$asymp.UCL[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"])`], *p* `r ifelse(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "yes"], 3)))`) and without health insurance (*b* = `r round(slopes_sum$chronic.trend[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"], 2)`, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", slopes_sum$asymp.LCL[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", slopes_sum$asymp.UCL[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"])`], *p* `r ifelse(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(slopes_sum$p.value[slopes_sum$insurance == "no"], 3)))`), although the difference between these slopes was not statistically significant (*b* = `r round(pairs_slopes$estimate, 2)`, *p* = `r round(pairs_slopes$p.value, 3)`). Simple effects showed that the non-significant insurance status "gap" narrowed very slightly as the number of chronic conditions increased. Specifically, those with health insurance were expected to have more frequent physician's office visits than those without health insurance when they had relatively few chronic health conditions (−1*SD*; *b* = `r round(contrast_df$estimate[contrast_df$chronic_level == "-1 SD"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "-1 SD"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "-1 SD"], 3)))`), with the insurance status gap decreasing for those with an average number of chronic conditions (*b* = `r round(contrast_df$estimate[contrast_df$chronic_level == "Mean"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "Mean"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "Mean"], 3)))`), and those with a higher-than-average number of chronic conditions (+1*SD*; *b* = `r round(contrast_df$estimate[contrast_df$chronic_level == "+1 SD"], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "+1 SD"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", round(contrast_df$p.value[contrast_df$chronic_level == "+1 SD"], 3)))`). Thus, although both insurance status and chronic health were key predictors of physician's office visits, there did not appear to be a significant interaction between the two predictors. Nonetheless, the insurance difference in expected physician visits ***was*** largest among individuals with fewer chronic conditions and appeared to narrow slightly as the number of chronic conditions increased.

#### Discussion
Taken together, the findings suggest that older adults' healthcare utilization is strongly associated with their health needs, including the number of chronic conditions they have and their self-perceived health. For those who have made at least one physician's office visit, self-perceived health had the largest individual influence. Other factors, including insurance status, education, and gender also seemed to influence the number of physician's office visits. In particular, being insured, having a greater number of chronic health conditions, and being female were associated with much lower odds of having visited a physician's office zero times.

The main limitation is that the cross-sectional nature of these data prevent causal conclusions. It is possible that the number of physician's office visits is associated with the number of chronic health conditions as a predictor, outcome, or both. It is also possible that other variables not included in this analysis could play key roles in predicting the number of visits, both independently and as mediators/moderators. The use of self-report measures (e.g., self-perceived health status) may have also biased conclusions drawn from the data. Finally, the results are somewhat limited in their generalizability, as these data were taken specifically from older adults living in the U.S. Thus, it is not reasonable to extrapolate the findings outlined here to other populations.
